fields.reasoning: All four recommendations follow the change set's intent text, which the owner filed with "yes file it": it names maxLoad per core (about 3.0) and minMemory (about 2G) beside minFree, hysteresis that holds above the limit and resumes only when the 5-minute average is back under it, Linux /proc/loadavg and MemAvailable, macOS sysctl vm.loadavg or skipping the check where unsupported, and a health/inbox threshold of e.g. 30 minutes. m4-orchestrated-by-rhiza is the fitting intent: its statement is the daemon orchestrating with no orchestrator session, and the evidence is the orchestrator hand-tuning maxRuns eight times on 2026-11-08..10. Skipping memory on macOS avoids parsing vm_stat page counts for a check the VM (Linux) is what needs; the disk guard already skips off unix (internal/daemon/disk_other.go), so skipping where unsupported matches existing practice. A fixed 30-minute threshold keeps the settings surface small; it can become a setting later if needed. Memory needs no separate hysteresis window since MemAvailable is a point reading and the run-start cadence already damps flapping.
fields.statement: The change set serves @{01M61R4RCY7AE9N46F2YDNX0WD}. The daemon holds new runs when the 1-minute load per core is over rhiza.daemon.maxLoad (default 3.0) and releases only once the 5-minute load per core is back under it; it holds while MemAvailable is under rhiza.daemon.minMemory (default 2G) and releases once it is back at or over it; 0 or empty disables each. Linux reads /proc/loadavg and MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo; macOS reads load via sysctl vm.loadavg and skips the memory check; other platforms skip both, and rhiza daemon status says the reading is unavailable. rhiza daemon status and the daemon log show every hold and release at once; rhiza health and the inbox report a load or memory hold once it has lasted 30 minutes, a fixed threshold with no setting.
